lead: After this unit you can look at a blurred, noisy photograph and say what degraded it, choose a filter that removes the noise without wiping out edges, and undo the blur wherever undo is possible. You can also rebuild a cross-section from its projections, the way a CT scanner does, and squeeze an image down to a fraction of its size with JPEG-style coding.
about: The unit has two halves. Chapters 3.1 to 3.6 repair a degraded image: 3.1 gives the model g = Hf + n, 3.2 describes the noise term, 3.3 the spatial filters used when there is only noise, 3.4 notches out periodic interference in the spectrum, 3.5 undoes the blur with inverse and Wiener filters, and 3.6 rebuilds an image from projections. Chapters 3.7 to 3.9 go the other way and shrink the image: 3.7 defines the three redundancies and how to measure them, 3.8 codes symbols with Huffman, arithmetic and run-length coding, and 3.9 finishes with predictive coding, the DCT and the JPEG family of standards.

chapters.idea: Every observed image is the true image passed through a degradation H with noise n added, so g(x,y) = H[f(x,y)] + n(x,y), and restoration means estimating H and n and then undoing them.
chapters.depth: Draw the full degradation-restoration block diagram. Take H as linear and shift-invariant, so it becomes convolution with the point spread function h(x,y); give both the spatial form g = h*f + n and the frequency form G(u,v) = H(u,v)F(u,v) + N(u,v). Cover the properties of the model (linearity, shift invariance, h as the response to a point source) and the ways of estimating h: from an image of a point source, from a blurred line or edge, from a physical model (uniform motion blur, out-of-focus Gaussian), and by experiment. Contrast restoration with enhancement (objective vs subjective). Some syllabi call this 'the model of the image degradation/restoration process'.

figure.title: Degradation and restoration
figure.aria: A chain from the true image through the blur H, the added noise, the observed image and the restoration stage to the estimate.

chapters.example: A camera moves 4 pixels horizontally while the shutter is open, so each pixel value is the average of 4 positions. (a) Write h(x). (b) For a 256-pixel row, at which frequencies does H(u) = 0? (c) What does that mean for an inverse filter? Answer: h = [1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4]; H(u) = (1/4)sinc-like sum with zeros at u = 256/4 = 64, 128 and 192; those three frequencies carry no information, so 1/H is infinite there and the inverse filter fails.
chapters.trap: Writing noise before the blur, g = H[f + n], which colours the noise; the order is blur first, then add noise. A second trap is treating restoration as the same thing as enhancement.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: convolution, correlation and the discrete Fourier transform.
chapters.leave: The statistics of n go to 3.2; the filters that use H go to 3.3 to 3.5.

chapters.idea: Noise is a random signal with a probability density, and the shape of that density decides which filter can remove it.
chapters.depth: Give the spatial model g = f + n for additive noise and mention multiplicative noise in one line. Present the PDFs with their mean and variance: Gaussian, Rayleigh, gamma (Erlang), exponential, uniform, and impulse noise in its bipolar (salt and pepper) and unipolar forms. Say where each comes from physically: thermal sensor noise is Gaussian, laser and ultrasound speckle is Rayleigh or gamma, faulty switching and dust give impulses, quantisation gives uniform. Show how to estimate the parameters from a small flat patch by taking the mean and variance of its histogram. Mention that periodic noise does not fit these PDFs and gets its own treatment.

figure.aria: Three density curves centred on zero: a narrow Gaussian, a wider Gaussian and a Laplace curve with heavier tails.

chapters.example: A flat 3×3 patch reads 8, 10, 12, 10, 12, 14, 12, 14, 16. Estimate the noise. Mean = 108/9 = 12 grey levels; squared deviations are 16, 4, 0, 4, 0, 4, 0, 4, 16, so variance = 48/9 = 5.33 and σ = 2.31 grey levels. The patch is symmetric about 12, so a Gaussian model with mean 12 and σ ≈ 2.3 is a fair fit.
chapters.trap: Reporting the variance of the whole image as the noise variance. Measure on a flat patch only, and remember the impulse noise has no useful variance, so a mean filter is the wrong tool for it.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for where n enters the model; Unit 2 histograms.
chapters.leave: Filters for each density go to 3.3; the spectral spike case goes to 3.4.

chapters.idea: When there is only noise (H = identity), the filter you choose should match the noise: averaging kills Gaussian noise but blurs, order statistics remove impulses without blurring, and adaptive filters vary their strength with the local variance.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this topic at this depth, so keep it compact. Cover the mean family with formulas: arithmetic, geometric, harmonic and contraharmonic with order Q. Cover order-statistic filters: median, max, min, midpoint and alpha-trimmed mean. Cover the adaptive local noise reduction filter f̂ = g − (σ²ₙ/σ²_L)(g − m_L) and the adaptive median filter with its growing window. Give a short table of which filter suits which noise and the effect of window size.

figure.title: One impulse in a 3×3 window
figure.aria: A 3×3 window holding one very bright pixel, the same nine values sorted, and the arithmetic mean, median and midpoint results.

chapters.example: The 3×3 window is 10, 12, 11 / 9, 255, 10 / 11, 10, 12. The true value is about 11 and 255 is an impulse. Sum = 340, so the arithmetic mean is 340/9 = 37.8, badly wrong. Sorted: 9, 10, 10, 10, 11, 11, 12, 12, 255; the median is the 5th value = 11, correct. The midpoint is (9 + 255)/2 = 132, also wrong. Conclusion: median wins for impulse noise.
chapters.trap: Using a mean filter on salt-and-pepper noise, which smears the impulse over the whole window instead of deleting it. In the adaptive filter, note the weight σ²ₙ/σ²_L goes to 1 in flat regions and to 0 at edges — not the other way round.
chapters.prereq: 3.2 for noise types; Unit 2 smoothing filters and neighbourhood operations.
chapters.leave: Noise in the frequency domain goes to 3.4; the case where H is not identity goes to 3.5.

chapters.idea: Periodic noise becomes a pair of bright spikes away from the centre of the spectrum, so a notch filter that zeroes those spikes and nothing else removes it cleanly.
chapters.depth: Explain the physical source: electrical or mechanical interference picked up during acquisition, which adds a sinusoid to the image. A sinusoid of frequency (u₀,v₀) gives two impulses in the spectrum. Cover ideal, Butterworth and Gaussian notch filters, the notch pass filter, and their band-reject and band-pass forms. Stress that the DFT of a real image is conjugate symmetric, so notches must be placed in pairs at (u₀,v₀) and (N−u₀, M−v₀). Show the recipe: take the log magnitude spectrum, find the spikes, multiply by the notch mask, inverse transform.

figure.title: Notch filtering
figure.aria: A chain from the noisy image through the DFT, the log spectrum with two spikes, the notch mask, the inverse DFT and the clean image.

chapters.example: A 256×256 image shows vertical stripes with a period of 8 pixels. The interference frequency is u₀ = N/T = 256/8 = 32. Its spikes sit at (u,v) = (32,0) and, by symmetry, (224,0). Place a notch of radius 2 at both points, multiply the spectrum by the mask, and inverse transform. Notching only (32,0) leaves half the interference, and the result is still visible.
chapters.trap: Notching a single spike and forgetting its conjugate partner. A second trap is notching the origin, which removes the DC term and turns the image grey.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 frequency-domain filtering; 3.2 for why periodic noise is not covered by the PDF models.
chapters.leave: Blur removal by H goes to 3.5.

chapters.idea: Inverse filtering divides the spectrum by H and explodes wherever H is small; the Wiener filter divides by |H|² plus a noise-to-signal term, so it backs off exactly where the data is unreliable.
chapters.depth: Derive or state the inverse filter F̂ = G/H and show the failure: F̂ = F + N/H, so noise is amplified by 1/|H|. Then give the minimum mean square error (Wiener) filter F̂ = [H*/(|H|² + Sₙ/S_f)]G, define H* (complex conjugate), Sₙ (noise power spectrum) and S_f (image power spectrum), and interpret the two limits: with no noise it becomes the inverse filter, and where H = 0 it gives zero instead of infinity. Cover the practical constant-K form with K tuned by trial, and mention constrained least squares in one line.

figure.aria: Two gain curves against frequency: the inverse filter spikes upward at each spectral zero of H, while the Wiener gain stays bounded.

chapters.example: A row of H(u) is known and the noise-to-signal ratio is taken as K = 0.001. Tabulate the two gains, inverse 1/|H| and Wiener |H|/(|H|² + K). At |H| = 1: 1 and 0.999. At |H| = 0.1: 10 and 9.09. At |H| = 0.01: 100 and 9.09. At |H| = 0: infinite and 0. The Wiener gain peaks near 15.8 and never runs away, which is why it is used in practice.
chapters.trap: Dropping the conjugate H* in the Wiener numerator, or letting K be negative. Also remember H must be the same size as the image, usually padded, before you divide.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for H, 3.2 for the noise power; Unit 2 DFT.
chapters.leave: Reconstruction from projections, a different inversion problem, goes to 3.6.

chapters.idea: The Radon transform collects line integrals of an object at many angles, and filtered back-projection turns those projections back into the object by ramping up the high frequencies first.
chapters.depth: Define the Radon transform R(ρ,θ) = ∫∫ f(x,y) δ(x cosθ + y sinθ − ρ) dx dy and name each symbol. Give the properties: linearity, the symmetry R(ρ, θ+π) = R(−ρ, θ), and the sinogram picture. State and sketch the proof of the Fourier slice theorem: the 1-D FT of the projection at angle θ is a radial line of the 2-D FT at that angle. Write the inverse Radon transform in filtered back-projection form, with the ramp filter |ω| and its windowed versions (Ram-Lak, Shepp-Logan, Hamming). Cover digital implementation: sample θ and ρ, filter each projection, back-project with interpolation. End with Fourier reconstruction as used for MRI, where the data are already samples of the spectrum.

figure.title: Filtered back-projection
figure.aria: A chain from the object to its projections at many angles, the ramp filter, back-projection and the reconstructed image.

chapters.example: A 2×2 object is f = [[1,0],[0,1]]. At θ = 0° the projections (row sums) are 1, 1. At θ = 90° (column sums) they are also 1, 1, so these two views alone cannot tell the object from [[0,1],[1,0]]. At θ = 45° the main diagonal gives 2 and the other diagonal gives 0, which resolves it. Naive back-projection of the two first views gives [[2,1],[1,2]] instead of [[1,0],[0,1]] — the 1/r blur that the ramp filter removes.
chapters.trap: Skipping the ramp filter, which leaves a blurred back-projection. Also watch units: θ in the formula is radians while projections are usually collected at degree steps.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for the imaging model; Unit 2 Fourier transform and the Fourier slice idea.
chapters.leave: Reconstruction from a single blurred image stays in 3.5; compression starts at 3.7.

chapters.idea: An image carries three kinds of redundancy — coding, interpixel and psychovisual — and compression is the business of measuring and removing them.
chapters.depth: Motivate with sizes: a 1024×1024 8-bit image is 1 MiB. Define the three redundancies and the measures: compression ratio C = b/B, relative data redundancy R = 1 − 1/C, and bits per pixel. Define lossless and lossy compression and the fidelity measures MSE, SNR and PSNR with formulas. Present the source encoder model: mapper, quantizer, symbol encoder, and the matching decoder. Define entropy H = −Σ pᵢ log₂ pᵢ as the lower bound on lossless bits per symbol.

figure.title: Source encoder
figure.aria: A chain from the input image through the mapper and quantizer to the symbol coder and the output bitstream.

chapters.example: A 1024×1024 image with 8 bits per pixel holds 1024×1024×8 = 8,388,608 bits = 1 MiB. After compression the file is 256 KiB, i.e. 2,097,152 bits, so b = 2 bits per pixel, C = 8/2 = 4 and R = 1 − 1/4 = 0.75, meaning 75% of the data was redundant. Second part: symbols with probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125 give H = 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.375 + 0.375 = 1.75 bits per symbol, so no lossless code can average below 1.75 bits.
chapters.trap: Confusing the compression ratio with the redundancy — they are different numbers for the same file. Also use log₂ in entropy, not log₁₀.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 sampling and quantisation for bits per pixel; Unit 2 for the transform used later.
chapters.leave: The actual coders go to 3.8 and 3.9.

chapters.idea: An entropy coder gives short code words to likely symbols: Huffman builds an optimal prefix code from a tree, arithmetic coding packs a whole message into one fraction, and run-length coding collapses repeats into count pairs.
chapters.depth: Huffman: build the tree by repeatedly merging the two lowest probabilities, read codes off the branches, state the prefix property, compute the average length L = Σ pᵢ lᵢ and compare it with H. Note the limits: at least 1 bit per symbol and the code table must be sent. Arithmetic coding: keep an interval [0,1), split it in proportion to symbol probabilities, output any fraction inside the final interval; explain why it beats Huffman for skewed probabilities and how the decoder mirrors it. Run-length coding: replace runs by (value, length) pairs, with a worked bit-row, and note it helps binary and palette images but can expand a noisy photograph. Give decoding steps for each.

figure.aria: A Huffman tree for four symbols, with probabilities merged from the bottom up and code bits written on the edges.

chapters.example: Four symbols have probabilities a = 0.4, b = 0.2, c = 0.2, d = 0.2. Merge b + c = 0.4, then d + 0.4 = 0.6, then a + 0.6 = 1.0. Reading the tree: a = 0, d = 10, b = 110, c = 111. Average length L = 0.4(1) + 0.2(2) + 0.2(3) + 0.2(3) = 2.0 bits; entropy H = 1.92 bits, so the code is within 0.08 bits of the bound. Run-length part: the row 0000111000 becomes (0,4)(1,3)(0,3), three pairs instead of ten bits.
chapters.trap: Building the tree by merging the two highest probabilities, or producing codes that are not prefix-free (one code a prefix of another). For L, weight each length by its probability, not by its count.
chapters.prereq: 3.7 for entropy and bits per pixel.
chapters.leave: Putting these coders behind a quantizer is 3.9.

chapters.idea: Neighbouring pixels are highly correlated, so predict each pixel from its neighbours (predictive coding) or transform a block to concentrate its energy (transform coding), then quantize and entropy-code the small numbers that remain.
chapters.depth: Predictive coding: lossless DPCM with f̂(x,y) = round(Σ aᵢ f(x−i,y−j)), the error e = f − f̂, and why e has a much smaller entropy than f; draw the encoder and decoder loop. Transform coding: split into 8×8 blocks, apply the 2-D DCT, quantize with a table scaled by a quality factor, scan in zig-zag order, then run-length and Huffman code. Justify the DCT (real, separable, good energy compaction, no complex arithmetic like the DFT). Cover bit allocation briefly and the blockiness that appears at low bit rates. Standards: JPEG baseline and progressive for still images, JPEG 2000 based on wavelets in one line, and MPEG/H.264/HEVC for video in one line.

figure.title: JPEG-style transform coder
figure.aria: A chain from an 8×8 pixel block through the DCT, the quantiser, the zig-zag scan and the run-length plus Huffman coder to the bitstream.

chapters.example: A 2×2 block is all 4s: [[4,4],[4,4]]. The orthonormal 2-D DCT gives DC = (1/2)(4+4+4+4)/2 × 2 = 8 and all three AC coefficients = 0, so 4 pixels became one nonzero number plus zeros — that is energy compaction. Quantize the DC with step 4: 8/4 = 2, send 2, and the decoder restores 2 × 4 = 8, so this block is exact. A block of 8’s sent with step 3 would give 3, decoded as 9, an error of 1.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the zig-zag and run-length step, so the long strings of zero AC coefficients are sent one by one. Also don’t mix the lossless predictive coder with the lossy one — quantization is what makes JPEG lossy.
chapters.prereq: 3.7 for the encoder model and entropy; 3.8 for Huffman and run-length coding; Unit 2 for the DCT.
chapters.leave: Video and deep-learning based compression are outside this unit.
